unit.unitOverview: Say hello! This unit is all about older people in our family and our community. Do these pages with a grown-up. You can talk, draw, match, and tick. There are no marks. Just have fun, look carefully, and be kind.

outcomes.text: 2. Draw an older person you know
7. My questions for an older person

explainers.title: 1. Who do you know?
explainers.body: Talk with your grown-up about the older people in your life.
bullets: Who is the oldest person you know?
What is their name, and who are they to you?
What do you like to do with them?
What is one thing they are very good at?

explainers.title: 2. Draw an older person you know
explainers.body: Draw someone older that you love, like a grandma, a grandpa, or a kind neighbour. Draw them doing something they like. Take your time and use bright colours.

explainers.title: 3. The age line
explainers.body:
People grow through life in this order. Read it out loud with your grown-up, from start to end:

baby -> child -> teenager -> grown-up -> older person

We were all babies once, and one day we will all be older. The age line is for everybody.
bullets: Put a circle where you are on the age line.
Put a star where your grandma or grandpa is.
Point to where a baby would be.
Who in your family is on each part of the line? Talk about it.

explainers.title: 4. Young or older?
explainers.body: Look at each one. Say young or older out loud, then write Y for young or O for older.
bullets: A baby drinking milk. ____
A grandpa with grey hair. ____
A little child learning to walk. ____
An old woman telling a story. ____
A young boy kicking a ball. ____
An older man with a walking stick. ____

explainers.title: 5. Match to help
explainers.body:
As people get older, some things get harder for them. That is when we can help. Draw a line from each older person to the kind thing that would help them. Do it with your grown-up.

Answers to check together: 1-C, 2-D, 3-B, 4-A.

rows: 1. It is hard for Grandpa to walk far to the shop.
A. Sit with her and talk, or read a story together.
2. Grandma cannot hear the television well.
B. Read the small words out loud for him.
3. Uncle finds tiny writing hard to read.
C. A bench to rest on, or a shop closer to home.
4. Auntie feels a bit lonely in the afternoon.
D. Turn the sound up a little, and look at her when you speak.

explainers.title: 6. Being kind to older people
explainers.body:
Put a tick next to the kind things we can do. Talk about each one.

Now circle your favourite kind thing to do. Try it this week!
bullets: Say hello and smile. ( )
Help carry a heavy bag. ( )
Rush past and ignore them. ( )
Listen when they tell a story. ( )
Speak clearly and wait for them. ( )

explainers.title: 7. My questions for an older person
explainers.body: You are going to talk to an older person you know. With your grown-up, write two questions. A good question lets them say lots, not just yes or no. For example: What did you like to play when you were little?

explainers.title: 8. A story from long ago
explainers.body: Older people know lots of stories. Ask an older person to tell you about a game they played, or a happy day, when they were young like you.
bullets: What was their story about?
Was their life the same as yours, or different?

explainers.title: 9. A word to keep
explainers.body:
Older people know special words and wise sayings. Ask an older person to teach you one word or a short saying that they like.

Now say it out loud together three times. Keep it in your heart.
bullets: The word or saying is: ______________________

bigIdeas.title: What is an age-friendly place?
lines: It is a place that is easy, safe and pleasant for older people.
It has comfy spots to sit and rest, with shade.
It has smooth, safe paths so it is easy to get around.
It has kind people nearby, and help close by if it is needed.
Older people helped to build our world. An age-friendly place is one way to say thank you to them.

bigIdeas.title: A little thank you
lines: The name of my older-person hero is: ______________________
One thing I love about them is: ______________________
Today I will tell them thank you, or give them a hug or a smile.

Well done! You have been a kind finder-out this whole unit. Older people have so much to share, and you now know just how to listen to them. Keep being kind, and keep asking your questions. Older and wiser - and now, so are you!

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up)
lines: With your grown-up, say hello to your AI tutor.
Tell it about the older person you drew and what they like to do.
Ask it: what is one kind thing a child can do for an older person?
Talk about the answer together.
Well done! You are a kind finder-out. Older people love to be listened to, and you know just how to do it.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up)
lines: With your grown-up, tell your AI tutor one thing you learned about older people.
Ask it to help you think of one more kind thing to do for an older person this week.
Say thank you and goodbye.

speakingPrompts.title: Talk to an Older Person
lines: Ask your questions to a grandma, grandpa, or kind older neighbour.
Listen carefully. Look at them while they talk.
Write or draw one thing they said here: ______________________
Say thank you at the end.

speakingPrompts.title: Talk to an Older Person
lines: If you can, ask an older person what would make this place nicer for them.
Listen carefully - they know best what they need.
Write one idea they gave you here: ______________________

grownUpGuide.label: For the grown-up
grownUpGuide.intro: This part is written for the parent or teacher sitting with the learner, and is kept in their own words.

sections.title: Welcome to this unit
sections.body:
Welcome to Unit 3 of Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. This guide is written for you, the grown-up, whether you are a teacher or a parent helping at home. Your child is about seven or eight years old, so this unit is led by you together, side by side. You do not need to be an expert. You just need to talk, look at pictures, ask gentle questions, and do a few simple activities together.

The topic of this unit is older people in our family and our community. The unit is called Older and Wiser, because older people have lived a long time and know a great deal. Your child will find out who the older people around them are, what those people like to do, what matters to them, and how we can make our community a kind and easy place for them to live. Along the way, your child will begin to grow the thinking skills that Global Perspectives is all about.

In our part of the world, in Somalia and across East Africa, older people are loved and respected. Grandparents often live close by, tell stories, and help to raise the children. This unit fits our way of life beautifully, and it gives your child a warm reason to spend time with the older people they love.

sections.title: What your child will practise
sections.body:
Global Perspectives is not really about facts to remember. It is about ways of thinking that help us for our whole life. In this unit, we keep the ideas very simple and we do not use difficult labels with the children. Behind the fun, your child is quietly practising three big skills:

You do not need to name these skills for your child. Just enjoy the activities, and the skills will grow on their own.
items: Finding out - looking, asking good questions, and listening carefully to learn about older people. This is the start of real research.
Seeing another person's side - noticing that older people may feel, need, and want different things from a young child, and that different people can feel differently about the same thing.
Thinking back - stopping at the end to ask what we learned, what we enjoyed, and what was hard. This is called reflection.

sections.title: How this unit works
sections.body:
This unit uses the Ehel Academy way of learning for young children. Three kinds of help work together:

There are three short files for this unit. This Guide is for you. The Activity Sheet is for your child to talk, draw, match, and tick. The Mini-Project and Reflection file holds the final task, where your child plans an age-friendly place, and a simple way to think back on the unit.
items: You and your child, together. You lead the way. Read the lessons in this guide, then talk and do the activities with your child at a gentle pace. There is no rush and there are no marks.

Short teacher sessions, about twice a week. If your child is in a class, the teacher meets them a couple of times each week to share drawings, talk together, and check how everyone is getting on. At home, your family time can play this same role.

Your AI tutor, used together with a grown-up. A few times in this unit you will see a box that says Ask Your AI Tutor. For young children, always use the AI tutor with a grown-up sitting beside them. You type or read the question together, and you talk about the answer together.

sections.title: Meet Layla
sections.body:
To make the unit friendly, we follow a girl named Layla. She is in Year 3 at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. Layla lives near her grandmother, whom she calls Grandma, and she loves to sit with her in the afternoon. Grandma tells stories about long ago, shows Layla how to knead dough, and always has time to listen.

As your child moves through the unit, they will hear little bits of what Layla finds out about the older people she knows. You can invite your child to be like Layla: a kind finder-out, who asks questions and truly listens. Layla's friends in the story come from many different homes, which helps every child feel that they belong.

sections.title: Key words for this unit
sections.body: Here are the simple words your child will meet. Say them out loud together. You do not need to test them; just use them naturally as you talk.

rows: young
In the early part of life, like a baby or a child.
old / older person
Someone who has lived for many years, like a grandparent.
elder
A kind word for an older, respected person in the family or community.
timeline
A line that shows the order of things, like baby, child, grown-up, older person.
community
All the people who live and share life near us.
respect
Treating someone with kindness and care because they matter.
survey
Asking lots of people the same questions to find out what they think.
interview
Asking one person questions and listening carefully to their answers.
age-friendly
A place that is easy, safe and kind for older people to live in.

sections.title: What you will need
items: The Activity Sheet and the Mini-Project file, printed if you can, or on a screen.
Crayons or coloured pencils, and some paper for drawing.
Old magazines or newspapers to cut out pictures of people, if you have them.
A story or picture book that has an older person, such as a grandparent, in it (any language is fine).
Best of all: a real older person your child can talk to, in person or by phone.

sections.title: Teaching the six short lessons
sections.body: The unit has six little lessons, then a final task. For each lesson you will find an Aim (what it is for), a Talk about part (questions to chat over first), and a Do part (the activity). Take them in order, one or two a week.

sections.title: Lesson 1: What is young? What is old?
sections.body: Aim: to help your child notice that people are different ages, to put ages in order, and to see that people can feel differently about getting older.

sections.title: Talk about:
sections.body: Do: Sort some pictures of people into younger and older (use the Activity Sheet or pictures cut from a magazine). Then draw a simple age line together: baby, child, teenager, grown-up, older person. Point to where your child is, where you are, and where Grandma or Grandpa is. To finish, read a short story that has an older person in it, and ask: is the older person shown as kind and happy, or as sad? There is no single right answer.
items: Who is the youngest person you know? Who is the oldest?
How can we tell if someone is young or older?
Is being older a happy thing, a hard thing, or a bit of both?

sections.title: Lesson 2: How many older people are there?
sections.body: Aim: to find out, in a simple way, that people all over the world are living longer, so there are more older people than before; and to practise counting and reading a very simple chart in our own community.

sections.title: Talk about:
sections.body: Do: Share one simple, true fact with your child: all around the world, more and more people are living to be older. A few years ago, about one person in every eleven was over sixty-five. By the time your child is grown up, it may be about one in six. Then make it local and real. Together, count the older people your child knows: in the family, on the street, at the mosque or church, and at the market. Make a simple block chart, one block for each older person, so your child can see the number grow.
items: Long ago, many people did not live to be very old. Today lots of people live to be grandparents and great-grandparents. Why might that be?
Good food, clean water, doctors and medicine all help people live longer.

sections.title: Lesson 3: What do older people do?
sections.body: Aim: to notice the many different things older people do, and to practise asking good questions to find out more.

sections.title: Talk about:
sections.body: Do: Talk about the many things older people might do: gardening, cooking, praying, telling stories, minding little children, teaching, selling in the market, resting, walking, or playing a sport. Then help your child write three to five simple questions to ask an older person about what they like to do. Explain gently that some questions have a short yes-or-no answer, and some questions let a person say lots. A question like What do you like to do? lets them say lots, and that is a good kind of question.
items: What does an older person you know do in a day?
Do all older people do the same things? (No - they are all different.)

sections.title: Lesson 4: What is important to older people?
sections.body: Aim: to find out what matters most to older people by asking and truly listening. This is the heart of the unit.

sections.title: Talk about:
sections.body: Do: Use the questions your child made in Lesson 3 to talk to a real older person, in person or by phone. Help your child listen well and remember one or two things the person said. Afterwards, talk about the best way to remember what someone tells us: we can say it back to them, write down one word, or, if they say yes, record their voice.
items: What do you think is important to Grandma or to an older person you know?
It might be family, faith, health, friends, feeling useful, or being treated with respect.

sections.title: Lesson 5: What do we know and think about older people?
sections.body: Aim: to gather what we have found out, to say what we think now, and to imagine how older people might feel.

sections.title: Talk about:
sections.body: Do: Help your child sort their findings into two simple lists or picture groups: things older people like to do, and things that are important to them. Then ask: how do you think the person you talked to feels about being older? Draw a happy, an in-between, or a sad face, and talk about why. Finally, help your child say one little conclusion out loud, such as: older people are all different, and the people I asked care most about their family.
items: What have we found out about older people this week?
What surprised you the most?

sections.title: Lesson 6: How can we make an age-friendly community?
sections.body: Aim: to learn that a good community is kind and easy for older people, and to think of ways to make ours better.

sections.title: Talk about:
sections.body: Do: Tell your child that there is even a big group of people, called the World Health Organization (or WHO for short), whose job is to help everyone in the world stay healthy. They say that towns and villages should be good places for older people too. Share the four simple ideas of an age-friendly place, then do the matching game on the Activity Sheet, and let your child draw a poster of one good idea.
items: What makes a place easy and pleasant for an older person?
What might be hard for them? Think of steps, long walks, fast traffic, nowhere to sit, or feeling lonely.

sections.title: The final task: plan an age-friendly place
sections.body:
At the end of the unit, your child brings everything together in the Mini-Project file. With your help, they choose one small place they know well, such as their street, their home, a park, or the area around the mosque or church or market. They think about the older people there, and they draw and label a friendlier version of that place, adding benches, shade, a smooth path, a garden, or a helpful neighbour.

The final task is meant to be joyful, not hard. The drawing does not need to be neat or clever. What matters is that your child has thought kindly about older people and has one real idea to make life a little better for them. If your child wants to, they can share their plan with the family or with an older person, and even try one small idea for real.

sections.title: Thinking back together
sections.body:
The last part of the Mini-Project file is a simple reflection. Your child looks back at the unit and thinks about what they learned, what they enjoyed, and what was tricky. For a young child, this is best done out loud, with you writing or drawing their answers if needed. There are no wrong answers. The aim is simply to notice our own thinking, which is a skill your child will use for years to come.

Try not to turn this into a test. A few minutes of happy talk, perhaps over a snack, works far better than a long list of questions. If your child comes away remembering one older person and one kind act, that is a wonderful result.

sections.title: A last word
sections.body:
Thank you for guiding your child through this unit. By spending time with older people, asking questions, and thinking about how to be kind, your child is not only learning to think like a researcher. They are also growing into a caring member of the family and the community. That is exactly what Global Perspectives hopes for. Enjoy the stories your child brings home; some of them may surprise you.

You may even find that this unit draws your family a little closer, as old stories are told again and younger and older hearts spend time together. That gentle gift is the real heart of Older and Wiser.

project.title: Mini-project
project.intro: This is your big task for the whole unit. It is called your mini-project. Do it with your grown-up, one step at a time. You have found out lots about older people. Now you will use what you know to plan an age-friendly place - a place that is kind and easy for older people. Then you will draw it. Take your time and have fun.

steps.title: Choose a place
steps.intro:
Think about a place where you often see older people. Pick just one small place that you know well, so it is easy to plan. Circle one, or write your own:

Write the name of your place here: ______________________. This is the place you will make more age-friendly.
items: my street
my home
a park
the market
near the mosque or church

steps.title: Find out
steps.intro: Good planners find out first, just like you did in this unit. Talk with your grown-up, or ask an older person you know. Write or say your answers.
items: Who are the older people in this place?
How many older people come here - a few, or lots?
What might be hard for them here? (Long walks? Steps? Fast cars? Nowhere to sit?)
What do older people like about this place?

steps.title: Think of good ideas
steps.intro:
A big group called the World Health Organization (WHO) helps people everywhere stay healthy. They say a good place for older people has these four things. Read each one with your grown-up and picture it in your place. Tick the ones your place could have:

Now circle the one idea you like best for your place. You will put it in your drawing next.
items: Comfy outdoor spaces - shade, trees, and benches to sit on. ( )
Easy and safe ways to get around - smooth paths and safe roads. ( )
Friendly homes and neighbours - near shops and kind people. ( )
Help close by - a clinic or a pharmacy that is easy to reach. ( )

steps.title: Draw and label your age-friendly place
steps.intro: Now draw your place, but make it better for older people. Add benches, shade, a smooth path, a garden, or a kind helper. Label your ideas with words or arrows. Use lots of colour. Your drawing does not need to be neat - your kind ideas are what matter most.

steps.title: My plan in words
steps.intro: Now put your plan into words. This helps you explain it to other people. Finish these sentences with your grown-up:
items: One thing that is hard for older people here is ______________________.
This will help older people because ______________________.
The person who would be happiest about my idea is ______________________.

steps.title: Share it
steps.intro: Sharing is how a small idea grows big. Show your plan to your family, your class, or an older person you know. Tell them your best idea and why it would help. If you can, try one small idea for real, like putting out a chair, sweeping a path, or saying a kind hello.
items: Who did you show your plan to? ______________________
What did they say about your idea? ______________________
Draw a smiley face here if they liked it: ( )

steps.title: My older-person hero
steps.intro: Think of one older person who is special to you. This is your hero for the unit.

reflection.prompt: What did you find out about older people?
What did you enjoy the most?
Who did you ask when you needed help?
Would you like to talk to older people again? Why?
What is one kind thing you will keep doing for older people?

assessment.note: Stages 1-3 are assessed through the mini-project and the look-back grid; the source pack ships no quiz.
